exam: What immediate actions do you take when a patient develops fever and hypotension during a transfusion? — Stop the transfusion, maintain IV access with saline, assess airway, give epinephrine if anaphylaxis, and notify the blood bank.

How would you differentiate acute hemolytic reaction from TRALI? — Hemolysis shows back pain, dark urine, rising bilirubin; TRALI shows respiratory distress, non‑cardiogenic pulmonary edema, normal hemoglobin.

A patient has a positive antibody screen but a compatible unit is unavailable. What is your next step? — Arrange for phenotyped or washed red cells, consider plasma‑reduced components, and document the antibody for future matching.
Why is leukoreduction recommended in low‑resource settings? — It reduces febrile non‑hemolytic reactions and the risk of CMV transmission, improving safety where infection control is limited.
Explain the AABB grading of transfusion reactions and its clinical relevance. — Grades I–IV reflect increasing severity; grading guides urgency of interventions and reporting requirements.

A child develops volume overload after a packed red cell transfusion. How do you manage it? — Reduce infusion rate, give diuretics, monitor weight and lung sounds, and consider using smaller volume components next time.
What laboratory test confirms immune‑mediated hemolysis after transfusion? — Direct antiglobulin test (DAT) positive on the patient’s red cells.

How would you proceed if the blood bank cannot perform a bacterial culture on the unit? — Treat the patient empirically with broad‑spectrum antibiotics, monitor temperature, and document the limitation.

ai.summary: An exam‑focused overview of blood groups, compatibility, pre‑transfusion testing and blood products, with practical guidance for low‑resource settings.

b: Key concepts: ABO/Rh typing, antibody screening, cross‑match, and identification of compatible blood products.
sections.p: Blood transfusion medicine deals with the safe collection, testing, storage and administration of blood components to patients who need them.

b: Mild: transient fever, urticaria.
Moderate: hypotension, dyspnoea, hemolysis without organ failure.
Severe: organ dysfunction, disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Life‑threatening: cardiac arrest, severe anaphylaxis.
sections.p: Transfusion reactions are staged by severity (mild, moderate, severe, life‑threatening) using the AABB grading system.

b: ABO or Rh mismatch – most frequent cause of acute hemolytic reaction.
Allo‑antibodies from prior transfusion or pregnancy.
Bacterial contamination of blood components.
Transfusion‑related acute lung injury (TRALI) – often from donor anti‑HLA antibodies.
Volume overload – especially in children and patients with cardiac disease.
Febrile non‑hemolytic reaction – cytokines from stored blood.
sections.p: Most transfusion problems arise from immunologic incompatibility, but non‑immune causes are common in low‑resource hospitals.

b: Fever, chills, rigors.
Back or flank pain, dark urine.
Hypotension, tachycardia, dyspnoea.
Rash or urticaria.
Pulmonary infiltrates without cardiac failure (TRALI).
sections.p: Symptoms appear within minutes (acute hemolysis, anaphylaxis) or hours to days (delayed hemolysis, infection).

t.b: Confirms basic compatibility; mismatch explains acute hemolysis.

t.b: Positive DAT indicates immune‑mediated hemolysis after transfusion.
Elevated bilirubin/LDH and low haptoglobin support hemolysis.
Identifies pulmonary infiltrates in TRALI; if unavailable, use bedside lung ultrasound.

b: Sudden hypotension or cardiac arrest during transfusion.
Rapid rise in temperature >1 °C within 1 h.
New respiratory distress with pink frothy sputum.
Dark urine or jaundice within 24 h.
sections.p: Prompt recognition of severe reactions prevents mortality.

b: Acute hemolysis – give IV fluids, maintain urine output, consider steroids if immune mediated, monitor renal function.
TRALI – oxygen, diuretics if fluid overloaded, consider ICU admission.
Febrile non‑hemolytic – antipyretics; avoid repeat exposure to same donor.
Bacterial contamination – broad‑spectrum antibiotics, fever monitoring.
sections.p: Stop the transfusion immediately, then treat the specific reaction while supporting vital functions.

b: Report reaction to blood bank; retain the implicated unit.
Update patient’s antibody screen and consider phenotyped or washed red cells for future transfusions.
Educate staff on proper bedside checks: patient ID, unit label, bedside check.
Implement leukoreduction and pathogen‑reduction where feasible.
sections.p: After a reaction, document details, investigate cause and adjust future transfusion strategy.

b: Septic shock – fever and hypotension but no hemolysis; blood cultures from patient, not unit.
Pulmonary embolism – sudden dyspnoea but no infiltrates on CXR.
Acute kidney injury from drugs – oliguria without hemoglobinuria.
sections.p: Several non‑transfusion conditions mimic transfusion reactions.

DAT may be negative early in hemolysis; rely on clinical picture.
Stored blood may have low bacterial counts; cultures can be falsely negative.
sections.p: Laboratory limitations in low‑resource settings may mask problems.
